description: We’re a multidisciplinary team obsessed with Earth observation, code, and data storytelling, all united by a simple mission: making planetary data accessible to everyone. By bringing together earth science, heavy-duty data engineering, statistical modeling, and intuitive design, we turn massive satellite datasets into clear, engaging stories about our changing planet. 🌍🛰️✨
summary:
Iris is a web-based Earth science platform built to democratize the investigation of environmental change. Designed for students, researchers, and curious citizens, Iris bridges the gap between complex satellite telemetry and accessible, evidence-based climate analysis. It empowers users to investigate critical environmental questions- such as whether temperature, rainfall, or vegetation cover is shifting over time in a specific region.

The platform features an intuitive, scientifically rigorous workflow using natural language: users select an Earth observation variable, define a geographic region and timeframe, inspect interactive time-series visualizations, and evaluate whether observed shifts represent statistically meaningful trends rather than natural noise.

To lower the barrier to entry without sacrificing scientific rigor, Iris pairs educational resources with an investigative workspace. Users can start with the guided “Ask the Detective” interface, which translates plain-language questions into recommended NASA variables and workflows. Inside the workspace, Iris combines visual trend plotting with robust statistical testing, including Mann-Kendall tests, Sen’s slope estimators, and seasonal decomposition, plus AI-assisted dataset discovery.

Ultimately, Iris transforms raw, multi-decadal Earth observation datasets into clear, reproducible, and defensible environmental insights, equipping anyone to move from curiosity to validated scientific conclusions.
details:
Iris is an end-to-end, AI-guided Earth intelligence platform that helps people investigate climate and environmental change using NASA, NOAA, and other Earth observation data. Users ask questions in plain English, such as whether a region is warming, drying, or greening. Iris finds relevant datasets and, when live extraction is available, analyzes observations to identify long-term trends and anomalies. It presents the results in a clear, reproducible Earth Intelligence Case File with visualizations, statistical evidence, and data provenance without requiring advanced technical expertise.

How it works

  1. Natural Language Query Interpretation: Users describe an environmental question in plain language. Iris identifies the relevant phenomenon, geographic area, and time period, then translates the request into structured search criteria.
  2. Earth Data Discovery searches connected NASA, NOAA and other Earth observation catalogs to identify relevant datasets. Where live extraction is supported, users can specify the study area, date range and data resolution.
  3. Scientific Analysis: Iris prepares the selected observations for analysis and applies statistical methods to assess long-term trends, seasonal patterns, and anomalies. The results are calculated using analytical methods not generated by AI.
  4. Evidence-Based Case File: Each investigation is presented as a reproducible Case File with visualizations, statistical findings, data sources, methods, and provenance, making the evidence behind the conclusions clear.
  5. Accessible Environmental Insight: Iris makes Earth observation data and trend analysis easier to explore and understand, without requiring advanced technical expertise.

Benefits & Goals

Iris delivers immediate value by making Earth-system evidence more accessible, actionable, and transparent. It helps users move from broad environmental questions to clear, data-backed answers by streamlining the discovery, retrieval, and analysis of climate and Earth observation data. By reducing the complexity of working with large scientific datasets, Iris empowers researchers, analysts, educators, and decision makers to detect long-term trends, assess anomalies, and understand environmental change with greater confidence. Over the long term, its goal is to make Earth intelligence more widely usable, support informed climate and sustainability decisions, and advance public understanding of how environmental systems are changing over time.

User Scenarios

An Experienced Researcher with Domain Knowledge: A climate researcher is comparing long-term temperature trends across several regions but wants to avoid manually searching multiple data portals and building a separate analysis workflow. They use Iris to discover relevant Earth observation datasets, select regions and time periods, and review data quality before analysis. The platform’s visualizations and statistical Case Files help them examine trends and anomalies, document data sources and methods, and export results for further study. They can also explore related publications and use case studies to understand or communicate the analysis.

Amateur Earth Science Data Enthusiast: Dinodh is an undergraduate student who wants to research environmental change but isn’t sure where to find relevant data or how to program and analyze it. Using Iris, he describes his research question in plain language and discovers relevant NASA and other Earth observation datasets in one place. He selects a region and time period, then uses no-code charts and trend analysis to explore the data, save or download his results, and revisit the investigation later. He can also browse related research publications, learn from guided case studies, and explore global trends on an interactive 3D globe. Iris makes the process more accessible by bringing data discovery, analysis, and visualization together, while clearly presenting experimental features such as forecasting as exploratory.

Case Study

To demonstrate the scientific approach behind Iris, an Earth Trend Detective case study examined environmental changes associated with the August and September 2026 disaster periods in Nepal's Rasuwa-Trishuli region and the wider Narayani/Gandak basin. The investigation combined NASA MERRA-2 atmospheric temperature observations, GLDAS-2.1 snow and ground heat measurements, and GPM precipitation context across the period from 2020 to 2026.
After removing seasonal temperature fluctuations, the analysis identified a statistically significant warming trend of +0.15°C per year (p = 0.0016). The datasets also revealed an unusual February 2026 snow-water-equivalent increase of 423% above its historical February baseline, followed by elevated summer ground heat flux, reaching 9.10 W/m² in June 2026.
By examining these indicators together, the study highlighted environmental conditions potentially relevant to glacier instability and flooding. While regional observations cannot independently establish the exact causes of individual disasters, they provide valuable evidence for understanding environmental changes and possible contributing conditions.
This case study illustrates how the statistical analysis, visualizations, and multiple dataset investigations supported by Iris can make complex environmental evidence easier to understand.

Then afterwards we used our own website to analyze the data and to find a trend ensuring functionality of our website. For more case studies and comparisons visit the Case Studies page on our website.

Considerations

Our main considerations when participating in this challenge were how to make multi-decadal Earth observation and climate data more accessible, transparent, and reproducible, and how to increase the outreach potential of Earth system science to inspire curiosity among students, researchers, and decision-makers. We aimed to create a platform that is both educational and research-grade, bridging the gap between complex non-parametric statistical trend analysis and user-friendly, interactive learning.

The minimal, modern UI design was selected to cater to a broad range of audiences—from climate scientists and environmental journalists to educators and beginners—ensuring the interface remains intuitive, uncluttered, and easy to navigate. We also prioritized modularity and scalability, enabling the platform to process multi-gigabyte multi-dimensional gridded datasets (Zarr/NetCDF), support live API extractions across global NASA and NOAA repositories, and accommodate future analytical modules, predictive models, and spatial visualization layers.

Other considerations included:

  • User engagement: Designing immersive, interactive dashboards—including a 3D CesiumJS Living Globe, interactive COBE planetary views, and 3D seasonal orbit landscapes (echarts-gl)—to make planetary trend exploration intuitive and visually compelling.
  • Scientific rigor & customization: Allowing users to test and customize statistical methodologies—toggling seasonal treatments (raw, deseasonalized, STL decomposition, Seasonal Kendall), comparing robust Theil-Sen estimators against ordinary least squares, and controlling False Discovery Rates (Benjamini–Hochberg)—to foster hands-on empirical learning without statistical overconfidence.
  • Traceability & reproducibility
  • Education & multi-level communication: Providing three tailored explanatory registers (Explorer for general audiences, Student for learners, and Scientist for researchers), interactive educational checkpoints, and Super Intelligence natural-language catalog routing with clear guardrails separating conversational assistance from deterministic computation.

By addressing these considerations, Iris aims to make Earth system science, climate trend detection, and planetary observation more inclusive, approachable, and scientifically robust through modern web engineering, rigorous statistics, and geospatial technology.

Technical Implementation

  1. Front-end
    • Next.js 15 (App Router): Modern React architecture featuring server and client components, optimized asset streaming, and route handler proxies.
      • CesiumJS (v1.147): High-fidelity 3D geospatial virtual globe rendering multi-resolution raster tiles and Zarr spatial fields.
      • MapLibre GL & Mapbox GL Draw: Interactive 2D mapping engine with vector tile support and bounding-box drawing tools.
      • COBE & Three.js: Lightweight interactive WebGL planetary globes for navigation and spatial context.
      • Turf.js: Client-side geospatial analysis and polygon coordinate calculations.
    • Python Backend Framework: FastAPI (v0.115+) with Uvicorn ASGI server, featuring asynchronous endpoints, structured Pydantic v2 schemas, and background job queues.
      • SciPy & Statsmodels: STL (Seasonal and Trend decomposition using Loess), hypothesis testing, and anomaly detection.
      • PyMannKendall: Implementation of standard Mann-Kendall, Seasonal Kendall, and autocorrelation-corrected Hamed–Rao Modified Mann-Kendall tests.
      • NumPy & Pandas: High-speed vectorized array operations, data alignment, gap-aware interpolation, and date-cadence normalization.
      • Scikit-learn: Trend concordance evaluations and regression diagnostics.
      • Xarray & NetCDF4: Handling multidimensional climate reanalysis and satellite grids.
      • Numcodecs: High-performance compression and chunk decoding for spatial fields.
      • EODAG (Earth Observation Data Access Gateway): Multi-catalog search aggregation and federated access.
      • HTTPX: Resilient asynchronous HTTP client with backoff and rate-limiting wrappers interfacing NASA POWER, NASA CMR, NASA AppEEARS, GES DISC, NOAA CDO, and Open-Meteo.
      • Meteomatics API: 51-member ECMWF ensemble numerical weather prediction interface for 72-hour precipitation forecasts.
      • OpenAlex & DataCite REST APIs: Scholarly literature integration matching datasets with peer-reviewed publications.
    • Figma: End-to-end UI/UX architecture, design system design, color-blind accessible scientific palettes, and responsive wireframes.
    • SVG & Custom Graphics: Scalable scientific iconography, formula graphics, and platform visual identity assets.
    • Jupyter Notebooks: Statistical pipeline prototyping, NASA API verification, and Validation Lab benchmarking (VAL-01 through VAL-05).
    • Playwright (v1.65): Comprehensive end-to-end browser testing for UI interactions, map rendering, and workspace workflows.
    • Pytest: Automated backend test suites covering statistical calculations, accumulation logic, and error handling.
    • Git & GitHub: Version control, automated issue tracking, and collaborative multi-branch workflow.

You can view the documentation linked below for more detailed overviews of the web application, statistical methodology, technical implementation, and architectural workflows.

  • Documentation: https://docs.projectiris.earth

  • Contact Us : info@projectiris.earth

Use of Super Intelligence

We utilized several Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools and software throughout the research, design, and development phases of this project to enhance efficiency, accuracy, and technical execution,

  • Research & Literature: ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity AI assisted with statistical literature reviews (e.g., Hamed & Rao 1998), GCMD taxonomy evaluation, and NASA/NOAA API discovery.
  • Code Scaffolding: GitHub Copilot assisted with TypeScript typing, boilerplate, async error handling, and unit tests.
  • Catalog Router: An embedded assistant powered by Google Gemini Flash-Lite (gemini-3.5-flash-lite) parses natural-language queries into geographic bounding boxes, temporal cadences, and NASA/NOAA catalog keywords.
  • Zero-Hallucination Guardrails: AI is strictly isolated from data processing and statistics. All Mann-Kendall tests, Sen’s slopes, p-values, and Evidence Grades (A–D) are computed deterministically via SciPy, PyMannKendall, and Statsmodels.
